title: Verb and Preposition Contrasts: About and Of
summary: Distinguish meaning changes when hear, think, dream, complain and remind combine with about or of. Recognise hear from for direct contact and practise contrasts between news, existence, ideas, memories, decisions and reported discomfort.
learningObjectives: Differentiate hear about (receive news), hear of (know of existence) and hear from (receive direct contact).
Use think about for reflection and think of for ideas and evaluations, recognising contexts where either is possible.
Choose dream about for sleeping experiences and dream of/about for aspirations while understanding would not dream of.
Distinguish complain about from complain of and remind someone about from remind someone of.

explanation.heading: Hear about, hear of and hear from
explanation.body: Hear about introduces news or details you learn concerning an event or person. Hear of means know that a person or thing exists, even if you know nothing more about it. Hear from somebody refers to communication received directly from that person, such as a message or telephone call. Choosing the right preposition changes what the listener understands.
explanation.example: I had heard of the illustrator, but only heard about her exhibition after she wrote to our club.

explanation.heading: Think about an issue; think of an idea or opinion
explanation.body: Think about commonly means consider a question carefully or focus your attention on it. Think of can mean produce an idea, recall a possible answer or give an opinion about a person or thing. The question What did you think of it? normally asks for an evaluation. The patterns overlap when you mean someone is in your thoughts or you are considering a future action; think of and think about can both be natural there.
explanation.example: After thinking about the problem for an hour, I finally thought of a practical solution.

explanation.heading: Dream about experiences and dream of ambitions
explanation.body: To describe events seen in sleep, dream about is a common choice. For an imagined future ambition, dream of or dream about followed by a noun or -ing form are both possible. Would not dream of doing something is a fixed, emphatic expression meaning you would never consider doing it. A sleeping dream and a life ambition should not be treated as identical meanings.
explanation.example: While travelling, Mo dreamed about being lost at sea, although his real ambition is to become a pilot.

explanation.heading: Complaining about a problem and complaining of symptoms
explanation.body: Complain about introduces a situation or service that someone finds unsatisfactory. The listener can be added with to: complain to the owner about the noise. In a formal or medical context, complain of introduces an illness, discomfort or symptom being reported. In everyday speech, complain about a symptom is also possible, so notice the register and meaning rather than assuming an absolute prohibition.
explanation.example: Several guests complained to reception about the heating, while one guest complained of a severe headache.

explanation.heading: Remind somebody about a commitment or of an association
explanation.body: Remind somebody about an appointment or task often means prompt them not to forget it. Remind somebody of a person, place or past experience describes a resemblance or association that brings a memory to mind. In some ordinary reminders of dates or tasks, remind of is also possible; use a clearly described memory-triggering situation when you need to express association. A person receiving the reminder is the object before the preposition.
explanation.example: The smell of fresh paint reminds Lina of her first art studio.

comparisons.title: Awareness of existence versus direct communication

left.label: hear of
left.example: I have heard of the director but never met her.
left.note: The speaker knows that this person exists.

right.label: hear from
right.example: I heard from the director by email yesterday.

comparisons.title: Considering a problem versus producing an idea

left.label: think about
left.example: We need to think about the new delivery schedule.
left.note: The team needs to consider the schedule carefully.

right.label: think of
right.example: Can you think of a name for our new café?
right.note: The task is to produce a possible name.

left.label: remind about
left.example: Please remind me about the registration form.
left.note: The speaker wants help remembering something to do.

right.label: remind of
right.example: That wooden desk reminds me of my school days.
right.note: The desk triggers an association with the past.

examples.sentence: Have you heard about the new cycle path near the station?
examples.note: Hear about introduces news or information concerning a local development.

examples.sentence: The journalist had never heard of the small publishing house.
examples.note: Hear of expresses awareness that an organisation exists.

examples.sentence: I will think about your offer and reply on Monday.
examples.note: Think about indicates deliberate consideration before a decision.

examples.sentence: The young architect dreams of designing a public library.
examples.note: Dreams of + -ing expresses an ambition for the future.

examples.sentence: The patient complained of dizziness after standing up.
examples.note: Complained of is a formal way to report a physical symptom.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We have not heard of our cousin since she moved abroad.
commonMistakes.correct: We have not heard from our cousin since she moved abroad.
commonMistakes.why: Heard from identifies direct contact with a person; heard of describes knowing a person exists.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The announcer could not think a suitable word for the occasion.
commonMistakes.correct: The announcer could not think of a suitable word for the occasion.
commonMistakes.why: Think of expresses producing or finding an idea, including a word to say.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The owner complained for the broken window.
commonMistakes.correct: The owner complained about the broken window.
commonMistakes.why: Complain about introduces the situation that is unsatisfactory.

commonMistakes.incorrect: This old photograph reminds me from the garden where I grew up.
commonMistakes.correct: This old photograph reminds me of the garden where I grew up.
commonMistakes.why: Remind somebody of something describes an association or memory triggered by a sight or sound.

studyTips: Keep three separate hear cards: news about an event, knowledge of a person and a message from a friend.
Ask yourself whether you are reflecting on a question (think about) or generating an answer (think of).
Create paired contexts for remind: tomorrow’s obligation with about and a smell or photograph triggering a memory with of.

exercises.prompt: “Who is that painter?” “I am sorry, I have never ___ her.”
exercises.feedback: Never heard of her means the speaker does not recognise the painter’s name.

exercises.prompt: We have not ___ our former neighbours since they moved. They used to send us messages.
exercises.feedback: Heard from concerns communication received directly from the neighbours.

exercises.prompt: We could not ___ a suitable name for the new community newsletter.
exercises.feedback: Think of describes finding or generating a possible name.

exercises.prompt: The guests ___ the host about the unusually loud music.
exercises.feedback: Complain to somebody about something identifies the person receiving the complaint.

exercises.prompt: That familiar melody reminds me ___ my first school concert. (Supply the preposition expressing a past association.)
acceptedAnswers: of
exercises.feedback: Remind somebody of something means bring a particular memory to mind.

exercises.prompt: The design team is trying to think ___ a new name for the mobile app. (Supply one preposition meaning generate an idea.)
acceptedAnswers: of
exercises.feedback: Think of a new name expresses producing an idea, not deliberating about an existing one.

exercises.prompt: The patient was complaining ___ a persistent pain in her shoulder. (Use the formal symptom-reporting preposition.)
acceptedAnswers: of
exercises.feedback: Complain of is the formal or medical pattern for reporting a symptom.

exercises.prompt: After six weeks without contact, we finally heard ___ the organisers by email. (Supply the direct-contact preposition.)
acceptedAnswers: from
exercises.feedback: Hear from means receive communication directly from someone.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I have not heard of my cousin since she moved to another country.
acceptedAnswers: I have not heard from my cousin since she moved to another country.
exercises.feedback: The sentence concerns contact after a move, so use heard from.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The presenter could not think a word to describe the result.
acceptedAnswers: The presenter could not think of a word to describe the result.
exercises.feedback: Think of a word means generate or recall a suitable word.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The customers complained for the noisy air conditioner.
acceptedAnswers: The customers complained about the noisy air conditioner.
exercises.feedback: Complain about names the thing or situation that someone dislikes.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The sound of the sea reminds me from our childhood holidays.
acceptedAnswers: The sound of the sea reminds me of our childhood holidays.
exercises.feedback: Remind somebody of something expresses an association triggered by a sound.

speakingExercises.prompt: You received an email from your cousin this morning. Begin with “I” and use “heard from my cousin this morning” in one complete past-simple sentence.
acceptedAnswers: I heard from my cousin this morning.
speakingExercises.feedback: Hear from describes direct communication from a person.

speakingExercises.prompt: You do not recognise the name of a singer. Say one complete present-perfect sentence starting with “I”, using “never heard of that singer”.
acceptedAnswers: I have never heard of that singer.
I've never heard of that singer.
speakingExercises.feedback: Hear of concerns awareness that someone exists.

speakingExercises.prompt: A colleague offers an idea, but you need time to consider it. Reply with exactly these words in one sentence: “I will think about it.”
acceptedAnswers: I will think about it.
I'll think about it.
speakingExercises.feedback: Think about an idea expresses considering it before deciding.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the preposition in this sentence about a memory triggered by a smell, then say the whole sentence: “The smell reminds me from my grandmother’s kitchen.”
acceptedAnswers: The smell reminds me of my grandmother's kitchen.
speakingExercises.feedback: Reminds me of connects a smell with an associated memory.

speakingExercises.prompt: The team found an idea for solving the problem during lunch. Report this using “They”, “thought of”, “a solution” and “during lunch”.
acceptedAnswers: They thought of a solution during lunch.
speakingExercises.feedback: Thought of expresses producing an idea.

speakingExercises.prompt: A guest reported bad service to the manager. Make one past-simple sentence beginning “The guest”, using complain to the manager about the service.
acceptedAnswers: The guest complained to the manager about the service.
speakingExercises.feedback: Complained to identifies the listener, and about introduces the issue.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two complete sentences from these facts. First: the child / dream about / a storm / last night (past simple). Second: she / dream of / becoming a pilot (present simple). Use full forms.
acceptedAnswers: The child dreamed about a storm last night. She dreams of becoming a pilot.
The child dreamt about a storm last night. She dreams of becoming a pilot.
speakingExercises.feedback: A sleeping experience takes dreamed about; an ambition can take dreams of.

speakingExercises.prompt: You want a colleague to prompt you about tomorrow’s appointment. Make a polite request beginning “Please”, using “remind me about the appointment tomorrow”.
acceptedAnswers: Please remind me about the appointment tomorrow.
speakingExercises.feedback: Remind me about refers to a future obligation that you do not want to forget.

listeningExercises.audioText: I had heard of that photographer before, but I only heard about her new exhibition yesterday.
listeningExercises.prompt: What was new information to the speaker?
listeningExercises.feedback: Heard of shows prior awareness; heard about introduces the newly learned exhibition news.

listeningExercises.audioText: I have been thinking about the plan all week, but I still cannot think of a better idea.
listeningExercises.prompt: What has the speaker been unable to do?
listeningExercises.feedback: Think about describes reflection; think of a better idea means generate an alternative.

listeningExercises.audioText: The painted ceiling reminds me of the old theatre near my school.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three words immediately after “ceiling”.
acceptedAnswers: reminds me of
listeningExercises.feedback: Reminds me of expresses an association with a remembered place.

listeningExercises.audioText: Last night I dreamed about missing the bus, but my real dream is to run my own bakery.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which experience took place while the speaker was asleep?
listeningExercises.feedback: Dreamed about missing the bus reports a sleeping experience, unlike the future ambition.

listeningExercises.audioText: The residents complained to the caretaker about the broken entrance door, not about the heating.
listeningExercises.feedback: Complained about identifies the unsatisfactory issue: the entrance door.

listeningExercises.audioText: When I found the old map, it reminded me of our first camping trip.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why did the map matter to the speaker?
choices: It brought back a memory of a trip.
It showed the route for a trip tomorrow.
It reminded the speaker to buy a new map.
listeningExercises.feedback: Reminded me of describes the map triggering a memory of a past experience.

listeningExercises.audioText: We heard from our former teacher yesterday when she sent a long email.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two words immediately after “We”.
acceptedAnswers: heard from
listeningExercises.feedback: Heard from means received direct communication from the teacher.

listeningExercises.audioText: The doctor said the patient complained of numbness in both hands.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word verb phrase immediately after “patient”.
acceptedAnswers: complained of
listeningExercises.feedback: Complained of introduces a formally reported symptom.
